To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have developed a method for accurately estimating the axis/profile curve pair of an archaeological sherd from a dense set of 3D points, that our method works on 3D data alone, and that it does not require any surface normal information.
we have demonstrated that the surface geometry of a pot sherd, even when the sherd is small, can be accurately estimated by a simple axially symmetric algebraically implicit surface model.

(1) the axially symmetric implicit polynomials provide a very effective surface model for the geometric analysis and reconstruction of ceramic sherds; and (2) a robust, accurate, and automatic method for estimating the axis and profile curve of a sherd from dense 3D scan data is presented.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new method for the automatic and precise geometric classification of archaeological potsherds using dense 3-D laser-scan data.
developing a methodology for accurately and automatically estimating sherd axis and profile curves.
the problem of accurately estimating the 3D geometry of archeological pot sherds.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
our method is capable of producing accurate and reliable estimates of sherd axes and profiles.
the proposed method is an effective and practical tool for automatically estimating the surface geometry of archaeological sherds.
our method provides a precise means of estimating the axis/profile curve pair of an archeological shered, and, in doing so, it provides a means of estimating the geometry of the original vessel.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed a method for automatically estimating the surface geometry of a sherd and associated statistical error estimates.
we present a novel method for automatically and accurately estimating the axis and profile curve for an archeological shered based on 3D laser scan data.
we have shown that the surface geometry of small archeological sherds may be accurately estimated using axially symmetric polynomial models.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is now possible to automatically estimate the geometry of a sherd with sufficient accuracy that it can be used in an automated sherd classification and pot reconstruction program.
the surface geometry of a sherd may be accurately and efficiently estimated from 3D data, and the estimated surface may be used as the basis for reconstructing the original pot.

the estimation of an axis/profile curve for an archeological shered can be done automatically with high geometric accuracy, and that the estimation results can be used in the reconstruction of the pot from the discovered fragments.
